name: SNLI
summary: 10,000 sentence pairs labelled entailment, contradiction, or neutral by five annotators, written from photo captions by people who never saw the photographs.
overview:
SNLI asks an old question in semantics in its simplest form: given one sentence, is a second sentence true, false, or neither? The Stanford Natural Language Inference corpus is 570,152 English sentence pairs, each labelled entailment, contradiction, or neutral, and it was built because the earlier recognizing-textual-entailment datasets held a few thousand pairs at most, too few to train a representation learner. It was released in 2015 by Samuel Bowman, Gabor Angeli, Christopher Potts, and Christopher Manning and became the standard benchmark for sentence-pair modelling. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.05326)

The collection method is the reason the labels are usable. Each premise is a caption from the Flickr30k photo-description corpus, and crowdworkers were shown the caption alone, never the photograph; they wrote three new sentences about the same scene, one definitely true, one that might be true, and one definitely false. That gives a balanced three-way corpus in which the labels can be recovered from the text alone, and it sidesteps the coreference problem that makes entailment judgements between unrelated texts ambiguous: both sentences describe the same scene, so "a man" in one is the same man in the other. About 2,500 workers wrote the pairs. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.05326)

Progress on the test split traces a decade of sentence modelling. The authors' own lexicalized feature classifier reached 78.2% and their LSTM sentence encoder 77.6%; attention between the two sentences carried systems into the high 80s; pre-trained transformers passed the agreement rate between individual annotators and the gold labels, 89.0%, with the project page's catalogue of published results topping out at 93.1% for an entailment-tuned RoBERTa-large. SNLI is also the parent of a family of successors, including MultiNLI for genre diversity, XNLI for other languages, and e-SNLI for explanations. [Published results](https://web.archive.org/web/20261007202555/https://nlp.stanford.edu/projects/snli/) and [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.05326)
methodology:
This snapshot contains the complete official test split of SNLI 1.0: all 10,000 sentence pairs of `snli_1.0_test.jsonl`, with every annotator judgement recorded for each. The 550,152-pair training split and the 10,000-pair development split are not imported, nor are the Stanford Parser parses that the upstream records carry beside each sentence, nor the derived hard subset the project page offers separately. No premise is shared between splits, so the test premises appear nowhere in the training data. The 1.0 distribution carries no version history, so the archive is pinned by its SHA-256 digest; the data files inside it are dated 2015-08-17 and its readme 2015-08-29. [Dataset record](https://archive.nyu.edu/handle/2451/41728)

Each Task Prompt gives the premise, the hypothesis, and the question the annotators answered. Both sentences are reproduced exactly as published. The split holds 3,323 distinct premises, almost all used for three pairs each, one definitely-true, one maybe-true, and one definitely-false hypothesis by the same writer; premises average 13.9 words and hypotheses 7.5. The upstream caption and pair identifiers are deliberately kept out of the prompt, because the readme warns that they carry information useful for classification.

The Solution is the gold label followed by the individual annotator judgements, in the upstream order, with the writer's own label first. The gold label is the one a majority of annotators chose: this split was fully validated, so 9,990 pairs carry five judgements and ten carry four, and the labels are close to balanced at 3,368 entailment, 3,237 contradiction, and 3,219 neutral. For the 176 pairs where no label won a majority, upstream records the gold label as `-` and its readme says those pairs should be left out when measuring classification accuracy; they are imported with that marker and their judgements, so the split stays complete and the exclusion stays visible.

Keys are the upstream pair identifiers, such as `2677109430.jpg#1r1n`, which name the premise caption, the round it was written in, and the label it was written for. The importer uses only Python's standard library. It checks the digest of the archive, the label counts and premise count of the split, that every pair identifier parses and matches its caption identifier, that no sentence is empty, and that each recorded gold label really is the majority of that pair's judgements. It can be rerun with python3 data/snli/import.py.
scoring:
SNLI is scored as three-way classification accuracy on the test split: the fraction of pairs whose predicted label matches the gold label, over the 9,824 pairs that have one. There is no official scoring script and no submission server; the labels ship with the split, so every published number is self-reported. The authors also report two-class accuracy, entailment against contradiction, for comparison with older recognizing-textual-entailment work. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.05326)

Two reference points frame a score. The majority-class baseline is 34.3%, since the three labels are nearly balanced. The agreement between an individual annotator's label and the gold label is 89.0%, and 58.3% of validated pairs were labelled unanimously, with a Fleiss kappa of 0.70 overall and 0.60 for the neutral class; these are the figures usually quoted as the human ceiling, and current systems report accuracies above them. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.05326) and [annotation artifacts paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02324)

Benchopedia's sweep grades the 9,824 test pairs with a majority label. All 10,000 pairs and their annotator judgements remain in the snapshot.
limitations:
The hypotheses carry giveaways. A classifier shown only the hypothesis, with the premise hidden, reaches 67.0% on this test split against a 34.3% majority baseline, because the writing task leaves traces: words like `nobody`, `no`, and `sleeping` mark contradictions, added modifiers and superlatives like `tall`, `sad`, and `favorite` mark neutrals, and entailed hypotheses generalise over the premise with broad words like `animal` and `outdoors` and are shorter, with 60% of them at seven tokens or fewer. A large part of any reported accuracy therefore does not depend on comparing the two sentences at all, and the project page distributes a hard subset, the pairs a premise-blind model gets wrong, for a stricter measurement. [Annotation artifacts paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02324)

The language is narrow. Every premise is a crowd-written caption of a photograph of people doing everyday things, so the corpus is present-tense, concrete, and visual, with no dialogue, argument, or technical writing; the authors note that the premises are literal scene descriptions rather than the sentences a reader meets elsewhere. Conclusions about inference drawn from this split do not transfer straight to other genres, which is why the same group built MultiNLI. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.05326)

The labels rest on an informal notion of truth about an unseen scene. Annotators judged whether a sentence would be true of the photograph the caption described, without seeing it, so a pair's label can depend on what a reader assumes about the scene; neutral is the least agreed class, at a Fleiss kappa of 0.60, and 176 test pairs have no majority label at all. Accuracy above 89.0% should be read with that in mind, since it exceeds how often one annotator agrees with the consensus. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.05326)

The split has been public since 2015, is one of the most widely used datasets in the field, and carries no canary string, so a model may have seen these pairs and their labels in training, including through the successor corpora that reuse this format. There is no held-out portion that avoids this.
